analysis.one_liner: Raises fines on hospitals that hide their standard prices from the public.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate HELP Committee without a vote, a cosponsor, or any action after its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have imposed much larger fines on hospitals that fail to publish their standard prices for services, as federal rules already require. It would also bar hospitals from hiding those price pages from online search results, require annual price updates, and force the government to publish a public list of hospitals that are out of compliance. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Patients shopping for care, and anyone who wants to compare hospital prices before getting a bill. Currently the federal rule requiring hospitals to post standard charges carries a maximum penalty of only about $300 per day, so many hospitals ignore it; this bill would raise the fine to up to $600 per day for small hospitals, $20 per bed per day for mid-sized ones, and $11,000 per day for large hospitals, and would name noncompliant hospitals publicly. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have sharply raised the monetary penalties for hospitals that do not publish and update a list of their standard charges for items and services, making the existing transparency rule meaningful for hospitals that treat noncompliance fines as a minor cost.

It set specific fines by hospital size: up to $600 per day for hospitals with 30 or fewer beds, $20 per bed per day for hospitals with 31 to 550 beds, and $11,000 per day for hospitals with more than 550 beds, with payment due within 60 days of a final penalty notice.
It would have prohibited hospitals from using webpage coding to shield their required price information from online search results, so patients could actually find the prices.

It required the Secretary of Health and Human Services to publish a list of every noncompliant hospital, starting 280 days after the COVID-19 public health emergency ended and every 180 days after that, creating public accountability on top of fines.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals that do not comply with the price transparency rule, especially large ones, would bear fines of up to $11,000 per day, plus the administrative cost of publishing and updating machine-readable price lists every year. [S3]

drawbacks.text: Even the top penalty is modest for big hospital systems: $11,000 per day is roughly $4 million a year, a small sum for hospital chains with billion-dollar revenues, so the enforcement teeth may still be too weak to change behavior at the largest institutions.

Publishing standard charges does not by itself lower anyone's bill. Posted 'standard charges' are often far above what insurers actually pay, and the bill contains no requirement that insurers disclose negotiated rates or that hospitals charge patients the lower of posted or negotiated prices.

The bill's compliance clock was tied to the end of the COVID-19 public health emergency, an unpredictable trigger, and hospitals would have had 100 days after that date before fines could attach, delaying any enforcement.
Small rural hospitals operating on thin margins would have faced fines up to $600 per day, which some would argue adds compliance burden to facilities already struggling financially.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real gap: the existing hospital price transparency rule exists on paper but the maximum fine of about $300 per day gives large hospitals little reason to comply, and many have not. Raising fines and publicly naming violators is a low-cost, direct way to make that rule real for patients. The main weaknesses are that even the higher fines are small relative to large hospital systems' revenues, and that transparency alone does not force hospitals to charge less. The bill never got far enough for anyone to weigh these trade-offs in a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Kennedy introduced the bill on March 3, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill carried support from a single member of the 50-member Republican conference.
The HELP Committee took no further action, holding no markup or vote, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals that do not publish their standard charges are better off, because the threat of much larger fines and public naming never became law. Patients gained nothing beyond the existing, weakly enforced transparency rule.

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the HELP Committee.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Patty Murray (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded before the Congress ended.

against.name: Hospital industry
against.what_they_did: The bill's fines and public compliance list targeted hospitals, and the bill drew no other Senate sponsors during its lifetime.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had one Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern ever formed.

industries.note: The bill would have multiplied the fines hospitals face for not posting standard charges, banned hiding price pages from search engines, and publicly named noncompliant hospitals. Hospitals' interest in keeping opaque pricing runs directly against patients' ability to know prices before care.

Hospitals posting standard charges gives insurers' negotiated rates a public benchmark, increasing pressure on both sides of rate negotiations, though the bill imposed no direct obligations on insurers.
